#1363. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

Then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

Liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have said all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

They are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

What he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

It’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

We have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

Florian Wirtz has scored or assisted in three consecutive games for the first time in his Liverpool career: 🅰️ vs LASK 🅰️ vs Brentford ⚽️ vs Villarreal https://t.co/woLWk2SGGL

It was a top performance from the boys. We were two goals down but the mentality was always there. We knew we were going to win.

It’s up there with one of the best I’ve played. I enjoyed myself and the team helped me a lot.

Whenever I get the ball and there’s an opportunity to go one v one or two v one, I believe in myself. I’ll just keep going and be ruthless.

Rio Ngumoha talking to Gabriel Clarke on Amazon Prime: “Definitely one of the best games I played. I enjoyed it.  Whenever I get the ball and go one v one, the more it makes the opposition worried.”

When he was reminded that he was the youngest Englishman to provide an assist in the Champions League, he said: “Records are amazing to break.”

And on playing on the right instead of the left wing: “It’s helped me a lot in training. Slowly I’m getting better on the right.”

And to hear the crowd chanting his name: “This stadium, we have the best fans. To hear my name being chanted is a dream.”

PSG’s 4-2 win over Barcelona tonight also puts them on nine points. Aston Villa, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Sporting and Real Betis are the teams playing tomorrow night with the opportunity to maintain a 100 per cent record.

Nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

On the other hand, they dragged themselves off the canvas and the night belonged to Rio Ngumoha. He looked dangerous every time he received the ball, set up the third goal, and received a standing ovation when he was substituted. Liverpool need to put that contract in front of him sharpish.

Still time for another hairy moment at the back for Liverpool, but Perez’ shot from the edge of the area is blocked and that will surely be that.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Just the three minutes of added time to play, and Liverpool are probably grateful for that.

Could Liverpool be in for a nervous finish? Their defence is caught square again after a run in behind from Ayoze Perez, and Oluwaseyi was totally unmarked at the back post to apply a simple finish at silence Anfield.

Cody Gakpo threatens to score Liverpool’s fifth with an overhead free-kick, teed up by McConnell’s chipped cross to the back post, but he could not keep the attempt down.

The game is meandering towards its conclusion now, though a Villarreal goal would make things interesting.

Another Liverpool youngster enjoys a taste of first-team actions: James McConnell is on for Nyoni.

2 - Rio Ngumoha (18y 52d) is the third-youngest player to provide multiple assists in a UEFA Champions League game behind Warren Zaïre-Emery v Milan (17y 231d) and Theo Walcott v Hamburger SV (17y 250d). Flying. https://t.co/CUbbleRhEJ

Perez hits the post for Villarreal with only Alisson to beat, but the flag is raised for offside. I think that would have stood had he found the net, Van Dijk may have been playing him just onside.

Ngumoha receives his standing ovation, lovely moment for him. He has strong claims to be in Liverpool’s best XI. Bradley Barcola replaces him, not the player Villarreal’s tired defenders needed to see.

That is surely game over now, Liverpool heading for three Champions League wins from three. Former Newcastle United forward Ayoze Perez is now on for Villarreal. Ngumoha will be replaced by Barcola shortly and I’m sure he will receive a standing ovation.

The game has been transformed, and Villarreal are falling to pieces. They were guilty of losing possession far too cheaply, but Wirtz deserves credit for finishing with an authority he has been accused of lacking. Well struck across the goalkeeper with his left foot, his first Liverpool goal since April.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Ngumoha has been Liverpool’s best player on the night, although Cardona sold himself all too easily near the touchline. Ngumoha makes the right decision to pick out Mac Allister with a low cross, and the midfielder converts with the simplest of finishes.

Isak then replaces Koumas immediately after the goal.

Alexis Mac Allister’s second goal but Anfield also singing about Rio Ngumoha. He went past two Villarreal defenders to create that one. He has been outstanding.

There will be time to talk more about Rio Ngumoha – this is his best performance in a Liverpool shirt, a coming-of-age night if you will – but it cannot be overlooked how Alexis Mac Allister has been transformed. He was unrecognisable last season but now he is every inch the man who was a major cog in the push for the title.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Tsimikas with a dangerous, driven cross from the left which is just beyond the reach of Koumas. Liverpool knocking on the door.

Nyoni’s standing foot was slipping, but he made a clean connection on his shot from range and it whistled just wide of the foot of the post. Ngumoha then has the crowd cooing again, with another drop of the shoulder to beat his man.

Gravenberch found himself sweeping up as Liverpool’s last man, there. The second half has had a more conventional feel, Liverpool making the running as they shoot towards the Kop and their opponents soaking up the pressure. A game of fewer chances since the break.

Always helps having knowledge in close vicinity: a quick discussion with Rafa Benitez about Liverpool’s set up for the second period. Ryan Gravenberch hasn’t been moved to play as a right-back, even though you might think that is the case. Liverpool, essentially, are playing man-against-man. It is going to ask players to be brave on the ball and composed when they are in possession, as the slightest slip will lead to problems. It is high risk and high reward.

Not enough power in Gakpo’s strike from the edge of the area and Gulasci saves. Ngumoha looking such a threat again, attracting the attention of three or four yellow shirts and winning Liverpool another corner. Former Spurs player Juan Foyth has just been introduced by Villarreal.

Liverpool more industrious when they lose possession early in the half. Nyoni then produces a silky turn away from pressure deep in his own half which elicits an “ooohh” from the home fans.

Gravenberch took the ball off Ngumoha’s toes in the box, and the Dutchman’s shot from a tight angle was saved by Gulasci at his near post. I think Ngumoha deserved to have the shot himself after more great skill to find a yard.

Wirtz replaces Araujo, which could mean Gravenberch at right-back.

Oluwaseyi, another of Villarreal’s Canadian cohort, is on too. He replaces Saliba.

Florian Wirtz has been readied for action and will soon enter the fray. You would think these will be the kind of conditions in which he will excel. He needs to. Liverpool are lucky to be level.

03:54 - Georges Mikautadze's opener for Villarreal (03:54) is the second-earliest goal Liverpool have conceded at home in major European competition behind only Elpídio Silva's strike in the 3rd minute for Boavista in the UEFA Champions League in September 2001. Cold. https://t.co/NvKmS5jLap

Dreadful first 30 minutes from Liverpool but they have woken up since, and now they are strong favourites to win the game from here. Iraola’s selection gamble backfired somewhat, but he may well get away with it.

From the second phase of a corner, Ngumoha did well to keep the ball alive and lift a cross to the back post. Cardona tried to usher the ball behind and made the fatal mistake of letting it bounce in his penalty area, and Araujo sneaked in to score from close range.

The goalscorer Cardona makes a mistake to let Ngumoha’s cross drift to the backpost. That’s Liverpool’s equaliser from Ronald Araujo. As soon as Liverpool have got their act together they have looked dangerous.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

The crowd were impatient with him early in the half, but Gakpo is looking more of a threat now, Cruyff-turning away and shooting in the box but Veiga was across to block. Just the one minute of added time to play.

Gakpo wins Liverpool a free-kick in a shooting position left of centre, tripped after Nyoni had carried the ball well through midfield. Too much air on the attempt from Mac Allister, who a couple of minutes earlier fired not too far wide from 25 yards.

Plenty for Andoni Iraola to be annoyed about, but as a spectacle this has been far more entertaining than initially assumed.

Really slick interplay from Villarreal again, and Moleiro’s shot from 25 yards is pushed over the bar by Alisson. You can pick holes in Liverpool, but Villarreal’s play deserves plaudits too.

Alexis Mac Allister grabs a goal back for Liverpool 🔴 Game 🔛 https://t.co/Ml9OYgbNq6

Liverpool have scarcely merited a goal but they have one via a set-piece. Alexis Mac Allister was up early at the near post and he produced a well-directed glancing header into the far corner. That changes the complexion of the game.

Great finish from Mac Allister. The opportunity for Gakpo to cross from the left - that won the corner - was made by Koumas’ hold-up play. First time he has really got hold of it and pinned the defender.

Another run from deep causes Liverpool’s defence problems, but Mikautadze took a touch when a first-time pass could have released the runner through on goal. More groans from the crowd when Tsimikas is caught on the ball.

Then Gakpo flashes a better ball across the face of goal, and Veiga glances it behind for a Liverpool corner.

Villarreal want a corner, and they should have one after a shot deflects off Araujo’s back. Goal kick given though.

Gakpo and Koumas are on the wrong wavelength, and there are groans from the crowd at another misplaced pass.

Liverpool need to dig themselves out of a hole now, Villarreal have cut them apart to score a simple second. Cardona, the left-back, with a run from deep, and Tsimikas was playing him onside. Cardona had all the time in the world to steady himself and roll the ball beyond Alisson.

Defensive calamity for Liverpool. Both Mikautadze and Cardona could have taken that through ball from Saliba and finished.

Straight through the heart of the defence 👀 Sergi Cardona doubles Villarreal's lead at Anfield 🤯 https://t.co/ZPHAkiLjN0

Liverpool far too easy to play through at the moment, Villarreal might not be an elite team but they have enough technique to pass and move well if given the time. Mikautadze lacks some pace up front, but has shown some silky touches. As Alan Shearer puts in on Amazon Prime: “Feels like a training match for Liverpool. So lazy. Where’s the urgency?”

Better from Liverpool with Nyoni driving forward and the ball almost running into the path of Gravenberch for a strike from the edge of the box. Villarreal diligent in their defensive work though, no clear sight of goal for the Liverpool players so far.

Anyone who is experiencing Anfield on a European night for the first time will be wondering what all the fuss is about. Aside from a couple of flurries following a Ronald Araujo tackle and a Rio Ngumoha dribble, it has been deathly quiet. Rafael Benitez, an architect of some of the wildest evenings here, is in the press box alongside Robbie Fowler and they are a reminder of how it used to be. Liverpool need to raise themselves to bring the crowd to life.

Ngumoha is the one ray of light for Liverpool so far, he has the beating of Villarreal left-back Cardona whenever he drops a shoulder. Gulasci palms his deflected cross over and Villarreal survive the corner.

The flag was eventually raised for offside, but Villarreal were in behind the Liverpool defence again after a misplaced Van Dijk pass. Liverpool have not got themselves out of the blocks at all. They have lost possession too cheaply and look vulnerable defensively.

Buchanan with a teasing low cross through the Liverpool penalty area, and the winger is justified when looking quizzically at his team-mates. If one of the yellow shirts had gambled they would have had a tap in.

Most of Liverpool’s attacks are being funnelled down their right so far, perhaps no surprise given that is where Ngumoha is stationed. Liverpool yet to test the goalkeeper, though.

Villarreal then throw a punch of their own down the other end, with Saliba turning and shooting at the edge of the box. Deflected, and Villarreal have a corner. Delivery is poor and Liverpool clear.

The Spanish team are moving the ball around with assurance, some nice touches from Saliba in their midfield (the Canada international is no relation to the Arsenal centre-back).

Hats off to Villarreal coach Inigo Perez, who is not wearing a hat or, indeed, a coat. Instead he is steadfastly ignoring the cold drizzle and treating this, from a touchline outfit point of view, like a warm summer’s evening on the Valencian coast. Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.

No need for Liverpool to panic just yet, plenty of time to turn this around, and Rio Ngumoha is going the right way about it. Quick feet in the box to beat his man and fashion a yard for a strike, but his shot is blocked. Ngumoha is playing on Liverpool’s right tonight with Gakpo on the opposite flank.

What a remarkable start. Virgil van Dijk has looked a gear or two behind everyone in the opening stages. One bad touch required Jeremy Jacquet to make a swift recovery and that misplaced header has now handed Villarreal the lead. Social media will be abuzz with scrutiny about Van Dijk now, as is always the case when he errs, but it won’t be taken into consideration that he has been one of Liverpool’s best players in these opening 10 games. What price would you make him to atone with a header at the other end later in the game?

Van Dijk has made two dreadful mistakes in the first four minutes and this time he is punished. Liverpool’s captain was trying to guide a header back to Alisson, but the ball shanked off his forehead at the wrong angle and dropped for Mikautadze in the box. The striker was free, and he finished well across Alisson. That was not in the script.

The Georgian No 9 for Villarreal Georges Mikautadze had looked so lightweight in the early duels with Virgil Van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet. They had muscled him off the ball more than once. That was a gift from Van Dijk and Mikautadze took it very well.

Ryan Gravenberch has started the game in a more advanced midfield role with Nyoni and Mac Allister behind him. The home team are yet to string together a serious sequence of passes in the Villarreal half.

Liverpool trying to harry their opponents early on, but Van Dijk makes a hash of dealing with a simple long ball forward. Villarreal’s striker Mikautadze took too long to bring the ball down and the chance was gone with Jacquet closing him out.

It’s another young Liverpool team fielded in the Champions League, but they should have enough about them to see off this Villarreal side.

We have two important wins for us but we cannot stop. A very good team in front of us and I hope we are at the level of the game.

Different circumstances. It’s out fourth game in 10 days, Florian [Wirtz] and Bradley [Barcola] have played almost every minute so we have to be sensible and the same with Alex [Isak].

I think he is doing very well [Leiws Koumas], or else we would not trust him to start these kinds of games.

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Kerkez, Wirtz, Isak, Barcola, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Laffey

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1361. Gattuso: ‘Feel like I’ve been at Lazio for 10 years, Frattesi is fine’

Gennaro Gattuso says he feels at home at Lazio and that it feels like he has been with the club for 10 years rather than six months, and has provided a detailed update on his list of injuries and fitness concerns, declaring Davide Frattesi fit to play against Lecce on Saturday.

Lazio return to Serie A action at home against Lecce on Saturday at 14.00 GMT. The Biancocelesti went into the international break sat alone at the top of the Serie A standings, one of two sides still unbeaten in the league after 11 matches, and they have only dropped points twice since the beginning of the 2026-27 campaign.

Up next for Gattuso and his players is a visit from Lecce, who sit in 14th ahead of kick-off with 10 points to their name from their first 11 games of the season.

Gattuso sat down for his pre-match press conference ahead of the Lecce clash on Friday afternoon.

Gattuso’s press conference began with a detailed update on Lazio’s injured players and those who have recently returned from international duty.

“I don’t have to assess Frattesi, he spent the whole week with the group, he’s fine. We’ll see whether he has a cold or something later today, but everything else he has done has been fine.

“The Danes arrived the day after their game at 18.30 and worked in the gym along with Belahyane and Dele-Bashiru. We worked at a low intensity yesterday but everybody worked as a team. I’m also talking about some of the injured players. Zaccagni has been working on the pitch for the last five or six days. He still has some swelling, but he’s at a good speed and we’ll see him next week.

“Nuno [Tavares] has started rehab in the pool along with Sutalo. Adam [Marusic] had a small relapse on the issue he had a month ago. We’ll be able to assess the condition of the injured players next week. Cataldi didn’t train yesterday due to a minor discomfort in his adductor. We don’t think it’s anything serious.”

Gattuso was asked how he plans on managing this next block of fixtures in the lead-up to Christmas.

He insisted: “We’re only thinking about tomorrow’s game. We’re facing a solid, well-trained team and that is not just by chance. They’ve earned seven points away from home by beating Udinese and Venezia and drawing in Turin. They are very dangerous from set-pieces. As always, it will be up to us to have the right mentality, the desire to be on the pitch and to play at a high tempo. It will be a very tough match.”

Despite sitting at the top of the Serie A table after 11 matches, Gattuso feels that it is still far too early to be making any sweeping predictions.

“We can only judge the standings in the last seven or eight games of the season,” he insisted. “We know these are all important matches and we have to play each one of them with the right level of respect for the opponent, then we’ll see where that takes us.

“I coach a team that has to take things one day at a time. It’s useless to sit there and try to make calculations. We all know the difficulties, it’s important to not make mistakes in terms of attitude or mentality.”

After his encouraging start at the Stadio Olimpico, Gattuso was asked whether he can see himself staying put for the long term and put an end to his chopping-and-changing of clubs.

“I love going around and getting to know different cultures and mentalities,” he replied. “My growth over the last few years is a result of all the traveling I’ve done. We Italians always thin that we’re the best, but that’s absolutely not the case. If you can take something from other cultures, that’s great.

“Honestly, I don’t think about whether or not I’ll be here in two or three years, I am only thinking about today and I feel comfortable here. I feel like I’ve been here for 10 years.”

Lastly, Gattuso was asked which of Lazio’s upcoming games he feels will be the most decisive.

He responded: “I won’t answer that because there’s not a lot to say. Tomorrow’s three points are worth the same as the ones in Turin, against Atalanta or in Frosinone. They’re different opponents, but let’s think about tomorrow’s match for now.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1360. What it's really like to kill a fellow athlete - and the terrible grief 'you carry for the rest of your life': The cursed band of haunted sportsmen reveal the nightmares that never leave them

Published: 21:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 22:15 EST, 19 November 2026

Towards the end of the Australian summer of 2014-15, as the country prepared to host the Cricket World Cup, I took a flight from Sydney to Hobart, Tasmania, to watch a Sheffield Shield game between Tasmania and New South Wales at the Bellerive Oval, a beautiful ground perched on the banks of the Derwent River.

Australian sport was still in shock. A few months earlier, Australia's Test opener, Phillip Hughes, had died after he was struck on the side of his neck by a short ball from a young bowler called Sean Abbott in a game between New South Wales and South Australia at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Hughes was treated at the ground for 40 minutes and then taken by ambulance to St Vincent's Hospital in nearby Darlinghurst in a critical condition. 'Feeling for Phil Hughes after being hit,' former Australia Test cricketer Dean Jones wrote on Twitter. 'He is not in a good way! Stay strong Sean Abbott. Not your fault, young man.'

The impact of the ball had compressed a vein in Hughes' neck and when it split, it caused a catastrophic bleed on the brain. Hughes had emergency surgery and was placed in an induced coma. He never regained consciousness and passed away two days later.

Hughes was a popular, talented, gutsy cricketer with three Test centuries already under his belt. A small guy with the heart of a lion. He was 25 years old. Cricket mourned a terrible tragedy – some called it the sport's saddest day and the agony of Hughes' family was hard to bear. But there was something else. There was an awareness that two tragedies were playing out in front of us.

Hughes was lost but the man who had bowled the delivery that felled him had been left behind, desolate and distraught. Many thought Sean Abbott, who was 22, would never play cricket again. That he would not be able to find the strength. But that was why I had flown to Tasmania. Because Abbott had found the strength.

Phil Hughes was the golden boy of Australian cricket in 2014, with three Test centuries already to his name, when he was hit by a ball bowled by Sean Abbott and died

Abbott visiting the Sydney hospital where Hughes was in a coma that he would never wake from, having suffered a catastrophic bleed on the brain

That February afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I sat among a smattering of spectators who watched Abbott walk to the top of his mark. His team-mates shouted encouragement to him. They were willing him on with everything they had and Abbott bowled his heart out.

'Beautifully bowled, Abbo,' one of the NSW fielders shouted after one ball to former Test opener Ed Cowan. 'That's a beauty, Seanie,' another yelled after the fifth ball of his first over, when Cowan jerked his head out of the way of a short delivery so fast he fell over. Only one wicket fell that afternoon. Abbott took it.

It was one of the bravest sporting performances I have ever witnessed. Because even though cricket had voiced its support for Abbott, the sport could not protect him from his thoughts and from the knowledge he had become one of a cursed band of sportsmen who have unwittingly caused the death of an opponent during a contest.

Sometimes, tragedy in sport is not just the tragedy of the player who dies; it is the tragedy of the opponent who must live the nightmare of what he has done over and over again in his mind. To those that it has befallen, they say it is a grief that never leaves them.

That grief, that sense of a double tragedy, was brought sharply back into focus earlier this month when Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono. The accident happened in the final minutes of a game in Spain's Segunda Division, when Owono hurtled out of his goal and collided with De Miguel in the centre circle. He was shown a red card for the foul.

There was an outpouring of grief for De Miguel. I was among those who observed a minute's silence for him before the Barcelona-Aston Villa Champions League tie at the Nou Camp the next evening. Tributes continue to be paid to him. Owono, meanwhile, has become a pariah. It is said that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house.

Owono does not appear to have had the same sympathy extended to him that Abbott benefited from. His challenge on De Miguel, a striker who had had a peripatetic career in Spain's lower leagues, was reckless and cavalier. For him, the struggle with guilt and responsibility and public judgment is only just beginning.

FC Andorra will play their first home game since the tragedy against Leganes on Friday night but when they run out at the Encamp Stadium, a neat little ground beside a babbling river, the Valira d'Orient, and in the shadow of the mountains that make Andorra such a popular ski resort, Owono will not be there.

Earlier this month Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono

Owono has become a pariah. It is said that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house

The goalkeeper, who has 47 caps for Equatorial Guinea, was given the maximum sentence of a 12-match ban by the Spanish Football Federation.

Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera suggested Owono's ban 'might feel light' to all those mourning the striker, who was 30 years old, while FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique, the former Barcelona and Spain centre back, said the maximum sanction 'puts him (Owono) in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened'.

No one knows whether Owono will feel able to return to football when his ban ends. Footage circulated of him in an on-field argument moments before the clash with De Miguel, and it was used to suggest that he was in an unstable state of mind.

Some have pressed for him to be charged with manslaughter. His Instagram account was deactivated after it was deluged with abuse, including messages which branded him 'a murderer'. It has been reported that his brother, who is also a footballer, has been the victim of abuse because of his association with Owono.

Owono has only communicated through a statement released by his club. 'These are the most difficult days of my life,' he wrote. 'I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to ​process what has happened. I feel enormous pain at the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and all the people who loved him. I know there will be many questions to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.'

I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies. His brother, Dermot, took his own life. He lost his daughter, Danika, to cancer when she was just 33, in 2019. And in 1982, three years before he won the world featherweight title at Loftus Road, he nearly quit boxing altogether.

In the 12th fight of his professional career, McGuigan fought a Nigerian boxer called Young Ali at the World Sporting Club in Mayfair. He still remembers the clink of cutlery coming from the diners who were sitting ringside that night. That sound still takes him back.

McGuigan still remembers the sequence of punches that put Young Ali down in the sixth round of the fight. He saw his opponent's eyes roll back in his head and a feeling of dread washed over him. Young Ali, just 21, fell into a coma from which he never emerged and died five months later.

I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan (right) about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies

'There was the horror of that and we sat and we waited and we prayed that he would be better and he never got better,' McGuigan told me. 'I didn't know whether I wanted to continue boxing. I thought: "If I can do this to somebody…"'

He shuddered when he talked about Owono. 'Other tragedies happen and other terrible things happen,' he said. 'Life is a struggle. Something like that, you never leave it behind you.

'It is something invisible and it depends how emotionally vulnerable he is. He may never be the same again but I hope he is able to overcome it.'

There are others out there in sport, still trying to overcome it. Think of Matt Petgrave, the Sheffield Steelers ice-hockey player who was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after his skate fatally cut the neck of Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson in an Elite Ice Hockey League match at Sheffield Arena in October 2023.

Think of Jochen Mass, the Formula One driver, who spent years blaming himself for the death of Gilles Villeneuve during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix at Zolder in 1982, because he slowed and moved to the right in front of Villeneuve. The Ferrari ran into the back of Mass and flipped in grotesque cartwheels across the track.

Think of Matthias Behr, the German fencer who killed his opponent, Vladimir Smirnov, at the 1982 World Fencing Championships in Rome when Behr's foil blade broke during a match, penetrated the Ukrainian fencer's mask and pierced his eye.

Think of Gary Cully, the Irish fighter, who learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves, had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August.

'What a character and a gent,' Cully wrote in tribute to Reeves. 'It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson died in October 2023 when opponent Matt Petgrave's skate cut his neck during a match

Gary Cully (left), the Irish fighter, learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves (right), had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August

Dr Victor Thompson, a prominent UK clinical sports psychologist, has studied the effect on competitors of being involved in the death of a rival.

'The biggest thing a player will have had to absorb normally is bad performance,' Dr Thompson says. 'Now he has to absorb the fact that he was involved in somebody dying. He will be trying to work out was it his fault? Is he to blame? And all of that, because the emotions are so high, gets associated with playing the sport in question.

'So when Sean Abbott thought about going out there again, when he thought about putting his pads on, or putting his kit on and being around team-mates or the smell of the cricket bat – it'll all be associated to that very traumatic day.'

University of North Carolina academic John M Silva III argued that aggression in sport is defined in two categories: hostile aggression and instrumental aggression. Hostile is when the main aim is to cause harm or injury to your opponent. Instrumental is aggression for a purpose, perhaps ball recovery or to sow doubt in an opponent’s mind.

The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy. Whether forgiveness is extended to or opprobrium visited on the competitor who has caused the death of another.

That interpretation was used against Petgrave, who was notorious for having a bad disciplinary record on the ice. Some likened the action which fatally injured Johnson to a kung-fu kick and drew a link between it and some of his past behaviour. He was mercilessly trolled on social media. Team-mates, and many ice hockey fans, leapt to his defence and said any suggestion his action was deliberate was fanciful. They said his unusual action in lifting his left skate high was a direct result of being knocked off balance by a collision.

Petgrave could not return to ice hockey immediately even if he had wanted to. It was a full 18 months before the Crown Prosecution Service and South Yorkshire Police decided there was no realistic prospect of conviction for manslaughter and that no criminal charges should be brought against the 34-year-old Canadian.

In the intervening period, Petgrave's family set up a crowdfunding page, pointing out that he was unable to work or to return home until the CPS had decided whether to press charges. The page raised nearly £20,000 from well-wishers.

The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy - as it was for Petgrave

Petgrave did receive widespread support from inside his sport, with a standing ovation at his Sheffield side's next home match, while he was beginning 18 months under investigation

'This has been the most painful and overwhelming period of our lives,' a message from Petgrave's family said at the bottom of the page. 'Watching someone I love go through this has been incredibly difficult.

'Despite everything, we are doing our best to stay strong, and the support and kindness from so many people have been a source of strength. We continue to recognise the heartbreaking nature of this situation, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected. We hold on to hope that this will soon come to an end.'

Petgrave now plies his trade in the minor league ECHL for the Indy Fuel, a team based in Fishers, Indiana. He is an ever-present this season, playing opponents like the Wheeling Nailers, the Greenville Swamp Rabbits, the Kalamazoo Wings and the Bloomington Bison.

'We understand the responsibility that comes with the great support we receive from this community,' Sean Hallett, CEO of Hallett Sports, which owns the Fuel, said when they hired Petgrave. 'We are confident he will be a positive addition to our team and our city.'

I wrote to the Fuel, asking if there was any chance of speaking to Petgrave. They did not respond. The reticence is understandable and, in many ways, laudable. Players involved in this kind of tragedy are preoccupied with respect for the victims' families and the sensitivities that come with such terrible grief. There is nothing they can say or do to make it better.

Sometimes, it is the other way round. Sometimes, it is the family of a lost loved one who find a way to ease the pain of a sportsman eaten up by shame for inadvertently causing the death of a competitor.

Mass, who died last year, blamed himself for the sickening crash that killed the most exciting, charismatic, talented, electrifying driver in Formula One. As Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track until he came to rest in the catch-fencing by the side of the circuit. He died of catastrophic injuries later that evening, aged 32.

Mass was absolved of responsibility. It was a tragic accident. Villeneuve was running hot after a disagreement with his team-mate Didier Pironi and was pushing even his own boundaries. There were any number of extenuating circumstances but Mass still blamed himself. He retired from the sport the same season.

As Gilles Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track

Despite being absolved of responsibility, Jochen Mass (pictured in 2019) blamed himself for the accident and retired from the sport the same year

It was years later when he felt a tap on the shoulder as he was sitting on a plane. He looked up to see Villeneuve's son, Jacques, the 1997 F1 world champion, standing over him.

'I felt so guilty about what had happened and then suddenly, there was Jacques,' Mass recalled. 'He said: "Jochen, our family – we never blamed you. It was a racing incident – just a wrong decision by the two of you."'

All the shame that Mass felt ebbed away. He found his own peace just as Behr found redemption by sheltering the grandchildren of Smirnov and his widow, Emma, at his home in Germany to protect them from the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Behr, tortured by guilt about the accident that killed Smirnov, had written to Emma 30 years ago but the letter was lost. When he did not receive a reply, he was convinced that Smirnov's widow blamed him for killing her husband.

They finally met when a television documentary crew brought them together and Emma reassured Behr that she had never held him responsible. Behr has suffered from depression and suicidal thoughts because of flashbacks to the fatal accident.

'They are always there,' Behr said later. 'Even if I go into a liquor store and see vodka with the Smirnoff label on it, the thoughts of what happened immediately come back to me. But now that I am playing a part in the lives of Vladimir's grandchildren, it has come full circle for me. It was a gift for me. I can finally give something back.'

Maybe Abbott has been trying to give something back all these years, too. Perhaps the fine career he has had is his tribute to Hughes. He has represented Australia in one-day and Twenty20 cricket and is the all-time leading wicket-taker in the Big Bash League. He has represented Surrey in English cricket and was part of Australia's World Cup winning squad in 2023.

Many had worried that Abbott would not play again after Hughes' death. Not your fault, young man. Easy to say, harder to grasp amid the grief and the disbelief. But there was an outpouring of support for him, including from Hughes' family.

Perhaps the fine career 2023 World Cup winner Sean Abbott (bottom right) has had is his tribute to Hughes

That afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I asked him about the day's play as he came off. He said he was happy with how it had gone. Afterwards, I sat in the stand with Abbott's team-mate Nathan Lyon, the Australia spinner, who spoke movingly about Hughes and about Abbott. At the end of the interview I thanked him for making the time to speak to me in such difficult circumstances. 'Too easy, mate,' he said.

Except it wasn't too easy. Inside, Lyon and the rest of Australian cricket were still in agony. Later that day, Lyon complained to Cricket Australia that he had not been expecting to be asked about Hughes. He was upset about my questions. I had made a misjudgment. Things were still too raw.

Lyon was comfortable talking about Abbott, though. 'The way Sean has carried himself through the whole incident, well, credit goes to him,' Lyon said. 'He is a very impressive bloke. I've got a lot of time for him. He will do anything to help anyone out. He always puts mates first. He always has your back. He is a typical good mate. I'm proud to call him a mate.

'I think (Abbott not playing again) went through the minds of a few of us. But natural instinct will come over and you do what you do best and if that's play cricket, you go out and play cricket. It's about being around your mates and the mates who are there with him now, they're the guys who are going to get him through it.'

Abbott has never spoken about the tragedy. He gave written evidence in January 2016 to the inquest into Hughes' death.

'I saw him start to sway and I ran to the other end of the pitch and I held the right side of his head with my left hand,' Abbott wrote. 'I remained on the field until Phillip was placed on the medicab and then returned to the changing room. Once in the changing room I felt confused and upset, I had a headache, people kept coming up to me but I cannot recall what they said.'

Much of the inquest was dominated by suggestions that Hughes had been subjected to a barrage of short balls and sledging. The inquest heard that Abbott's bowling partner, Doug Bollinger, had said to Hughes 'I'm going to kill you' at one stage during the game. Bollinger denied that accusation. Abbott was exonerated of any responsibility for the tragedy that unfolded.

Only rarely are there glimpses of the impact that Hughes' death has had on him. At a tribute to Hughes on the tenth anniversary of his death, Abbott broke down and wept at the end of the minute's silence at the SCG. One of his team-mates put an arm around his shoulders to try to comfort him.

Abbott at Hughes' funeral in his hometown of Macksville, Australia, in 2014

'The difficulty with boxing is that you are in this sport to hurt your opponent,' says McGuigan. 'Nobody believes - or wants to believe - that it is going to do lasting damage'

McGuigan says the pain never quite goes away. 'I had a love-hate relationship with boxing,' he says. 'The difficulty with boxing is that you are in this sport to hurt your opponent. Nobody believes – or wants to believe – that it is going to do lasting damage.

'After Young Ali died, I had to make a very serious decision about whether to carry on or not. I refocused and tried to make it a goal to win the world title and think about him when I achieved it. And the night I won the world title, I told Harry Carpenter through my tears that I was dedicating the fight to Young Ali.

'What happened in Tenerife looked like a terrible accident. Jesus de Miguel did not see him coming and he had no chance to brace for the impact. The outcome is the same as the outcome I had to deal with.

'I hope the goalkeeper will be able to come to terms with it. Sometimes, you can't. Sometimes, you are never quite the same, emotionally or mentally. It is the burden you carry for the rest of your life.'

#1358. Iraola confirms ‘very good news’ after Leoni return to Liverpool training

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says that it is ‘very good news’ to have Italy talent Giovanni Leoni back in training after a nightmare 14-month injury lay-off, but has confirmed that the 19-year-old will not be available to face Manchester United this weekend.

Leoni has recently returned to training with the Liverpool first team after suffering an injury on his first appearance for the club well over a year ago.

Though Leoni was originally expected to miss around nine months of action with what was originally reported as a cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, Iraola later explained that it was a complex issue with the youngster’s knee and that he hoped to see the former Parma defender return to training during the November international break.

It has been 14 months since Leoni’s first and only appearance for Liverpool, in an EFL Cup second round victory over Southampton last September.

Liverpool have recently shared footage of Leoni back in training with the Liverpool first team squad at the AXA Training Center in Kirkby.

Iraola was asked for an update on Leoni’s progress during his pre-match press conference on Friday, ahead of Liverpool’s upcoming Premier League clash against Manchester United.

“Very good news from both sides, the break was the best moment for us to introduce them slowly,” said Iraola, referring to Leoni and teammate Conor Bradley.

“They have started doing things with the team, not available for Sunday and we treat them carefully.

“We are in the last part of this process and I hope they can play in some weeks.”

#1357. Premier League clubs vote 18-2 in favour of footing legal bill for top-flight chiefs if Man City's sponsors sue them for defamation... with City and Nottingham Forest voting against

Published: 08:16 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 03:21 EST, 20 November 2026

Premier League clubs have voted to protect the organisation's bigwigs from any individual legal action taken by Manchester City's sponsors.

Instead, the clubs - including City themselves - will foot any legal bills incurred by a potential corporate defamation suit.

Daily Mail Sport understands there was widespread support from clubs to insulate Premier League chief executive Richard Masters and the four other league directors.

The vote passed with 18 clubs in favour, and City and Nottingham Forest against.

It is understood Forest opted to vote that way as they felt they had not been given sufficient information or enough time to consider the proposal and its implications, as opposed to representing a show of support for City.

The matter was the first item on the agenda at the Premier League shareholders' meeting in the Savoy Hotel on Thursday and was addressed quickly with limited discussion.

Clubs had a paper for the proposed rule change before the meeting and there was significant support to extend the legal protection to individuals on the league's board.

This marks the first time since the Premier League’s inception that insurance arrangements for its board members have been reviewed.

Premier League clubs will foot the bill if Manchester City's sponsors sue for defamation

In September, City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules after a seven-year legal process.

An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City inflated their revenues by £900million – disguising money from their Abu Dhabi ownership group as sponsorship revenue.

Etihad Airways, owned by the Abu Dhabi government, denied being ‘involved in improper commercial arrangements’ and said it was considering legal action in response to the verdict.

Meanwhile, another City sponsor, Etisalat - a telecommunications company - is also weighing up legal action.

City, though, maintain their innocence and are appealing the decision, which could see them relegated from the top flight.

#1356. A grant to hand out more grants — and build a research area

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Virginia Gewin is a freelance reporter in Portland, Oregon.

Grants worth up to US$10,000 will fund niche scientific problems.Credit: SimpleImages/Getty

Amid political instability and decreased funding for science worldwide, some non-profit organizations are testing whether and how microgrants — awards of US$10,000 or less — can spur innovation. The latest development comes from the Experiment Foundation, a non-profit science funding organization in Berkeley, California, which has launched the Field Building Accelerator to cultivate ingenuity hubs around specific fields of research using small, rapidly deployed grants.

The initiative will, in early 2027, award at least 50 individuals — called field builders — $70,000 each. The recipients, in turn, will design their own microgrant programme to distribute up to $10,000 to researchers exploring distinct facets of the same niche scientific problem. The grants will be hosted on Experiment.com, an online platform that allows organizations to advertise and fund research projects.

“We want to create a different persona in science — the people who can chart new research territory,” says David Lang, executive director of the Experiment Foundation.

The accelerator programme is open to proposals that broadly target oceans, climate, toxicity, future science and conservation technology, says Lang — reflecting the interests of its funders, including non-profit organizations such as the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation in Palo Alto, California. Prospective field builders must propose a name for the field, define its core questions and challenges, and identify at least eight researchers, laboratories or communities they would consider funding.

Judges will select field builders who they think are best placed to identify overlooked talent, back unproven ideas and bring like-minded researchers together. Ideally, says Lang, they will reflect diverse scientific perspectives, including early-career researchers, science journalists, science-fiction authors and venture capitalists. “There are people that build momentum in scientific fields, but they are different from the ones who are getting big publications or spinning out companies,” he says.

And, in a bid to take chances on unconventional ideas, the judges will not average scores; instead, if any of the two or three judges champions an application, it moves forward.

Although some might baulk at the idea that $10,000 grants are large enough to spur new research disciplines, others say it is time to experiment with new ways to distribute research funding. “If we really want to help to seed challenging, high risk, ‘who knows what will happen’ ideas, then small-scale grants are a good strategy,” says Brian Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science, a non-profit organization in Charlottesville, Virginia, that promotes transparent and reproducible science.

In 2025, The Science Foundation in Seattle, Washington, organized public donations to award up to $10,000 to researchers who have a compelling ‘what if’ basic-science proposal in the areas of mathematics, physical sciences and biological sciences. The foundation announced the second round of winners on 12 November.

Newcastle United manager Matthias Jaissle is reportedly keen to reunite with Ivan Toney, with the Al-Ahli striker emerging as a potential target for the Magpies ahead of the January transfer window.

The German tactician previously worked with the England international in Saudi Arabia and is understood to want to add a proven goalscorer to his attacking options at St James’ Park.

According to a Sky Sports report, Jaissle admires Toney and would welcome the opportunity to bring him to Newcastle, although the club could face financial difficulties completing a deal for the 30-year-old.

The former Brentford striker has been particularly impressive since moving to Al-Ahli, scoring 85 goals in 108 appearances across all competitions. His experience in English football could make him an attractive addition for Newcastle, who have struggled to find consistent goals from their current attacking options.

Newcastle have struggled to produce enough goals this season, with Yoane Wissa failing to make the desired impact since his arrival, while the club are also searching for a more established centre-forward.

Toney could be an ideal solution to their problems. The Englishman previously demonstrated his quality in the Premier League, scoring 20 goals for Brentford during the 2022/23 campaign.

His physical presence, ability to bring teammates into play, and clinical finishing could add a different dimension to Jaissle’s attack. A reunion with his former manager could also help Newcastle convince him to return to English football.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

However, signing Toney might not be straightforward. He remains under contract with Al-Ahli until 2028, and Newcastle are reportedly reluctant to spend heavily on an established player approaching his thirties.

The Magpies are also considering strengthening their attacking midfield options, meaning their January budget could become a major factor.

Much will depend on whether Newcastle can negotiate favourable terms, but Toney’s proven goalscoring ability makes him an interesting option for Jaissle.

#1354. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

#1353. Juventus receive double defensive boost ahead of Venezia

Friday’s reports confirm that both Andrea Cambiaso and Zeki Celik have returned to training with Juventus and that they should both be available for selection for Sunday’s Serie A match against Venezia.

Cambiaso missed Juve’s final match before the international break, a 2-2 draw away against Fiorentina, with a muscular issue, which ruled him out of selection for Roberto Mancini’s latest Italy national team squad for the November break.

Celik, meanwhile, had been named in the Turkey national team starting XI to face France in their final Nations League group stage fixture on Sunday evening, but limped out of the warm-up with a thigh issue.

According to updates from Gianluca Di Marzio on Friday, both players were involved in Luciano Spalletti’s training session this morning and both are expected to be available for selection when Juventus host Venezia in Serie A on Sunday (11.30 GMT).

Juventus find themselves in seventh place in the Serie A table ahead of kick-off against Venezia. They have won five, drawn three and lost three for a total of 18 points in the league thus far, 11 less than the current table-toppers, Lazio.

A match at home against the 19th-placed Venezia, on six points after 11 matches, is an opportunity for the Old Lady to return to winning ways when league action resumes this weekend.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1352. 'F*** the Pope and the IRA' chant lands England in hot water as fans are given suspended one-game stadium ban and FA fined

Published: 13:19 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 03:21 EST, 20 November 2026

UEFA have slapped the FA with a £12,500 fine and a suspended one-match away supporters ban after England fans were heard singing sectarian chants during their Nations League victory over Spain last weekend.

Some of the 3,000 supporters who travelled to Madrid were heard singing 'f*** the Pope and the IRA' inside Madrid's Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday.

As a result, UEFA have fined the FA and banned away fans from attending one UEFA match for 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour'.

That said, the ban will only take effect if England supporters reoffend within the next two years.

It is a fortunate reprieve given the Three Lions' next away fixture is their Nations League quarter-final, the draw for which is on Friday.

Meanwhile, the FA have committed to identifying those involved and taking action - which could see football banning orders imposed.

In a statement to Daily Mail Sport, the FA said: 'We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police who attend all England home and away matches to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action.'

England fans land FA in hot water over 'f*** the Pope and the IRA' chant during Spain victory

England supporters have notoriously sung the anti-Catholic and loyalist chant. In 2024, the Irish police urged travelling fans to 'respect local culture' before their Nations League match against the Republic of Ireland.

Fans were also filmed in Milan city centre on the eve of the clash against Italy in 2022 singing the same incendiary chant - just one year after their European Championship final defeat to the Italians.

Meanwhile, then England boss Roy Hodgson and the FA were forced to condemn supporters after the inflammatory chant was heard throughout England's 3-1 friendly victory over Scotland at Celtic Park in 2014. Around 5,000 fans travelled to the devoutly Catholic club.

The issue is not limited to international football. In August, Daily Mail Sport revealed that Chelsea wrote to supporters after a section of their fans were heard singing the sectarian chant away at Fulham on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

England boss Thomas Tuchel was asked about racism in his pre-Spain press conference.

'I never expect racism and the dressing room is the most anti-racist place on Earth and that's exactly how it works,' Tuchel said.

'I expect emotional and of course supporting fans from Spain for their national team. That's what I expect, but I don't expect racism nowhere.

'I'm shocked if it happens, and it should happen nowhere, and I'm the first one to stand up for these kind of values.

'My trust is that we have a friendly atmosphere, that we have an atmosphere who is clearly in favour of the Spanish team, and that football does what it does best: bring people together and not divide people.'

Newcastle United midfielder Jacob Ramsey has offered an honest assessment of his struggles at St James’ Park, admitting his spell on Tyneside has not met expectations following his £ 43 million move from Aston Villa.

The 25-year-old joined the Magpies in the summer of 2025 but has struggled to establish himself as a regular starter, with injuries and disciplinary problems disrupting his progress.

According to a report via Birmingham Mail, Ramsey has acknowledged a disappointing start at Newcastle but remains determined to show his qualities under new manager Matthias Jaissle.

Speaking about his experience, the midfielder admitted that several promising moments have been followed by frustrating setbacks. He highlighted his impressive contribution against Bournemouth, where he scored after coming off the bench, only to suffer another injury shortly afterwards.

He said: “My time here hasn’t been great; there have been certain moments where I have looked like I am about to kick on.”

The former Aston Villa star has endured a particularly frustrating period in recent months. His latest setback came against Everton, when he received two yellow cards and was sent off during Newcastle’s 1-0 defeat.

The dismissal was his second red card of 2026, further complicating his attempts to secure a regular place in the starting XI.

However, Ramsey has apologised for his actions and is eager to put those difficulties behind him. With Newcastle facing a demanding run of fixtures, he could play an important role in the coming months.

The midfielder has also expressed confidence in Jaissle’s ability to improve the team, acknowledging that the players need time to adapt to his tactical demands.

“We need to give it some time and the results will start to show.

“He [Jaissle] is a little bit different to the last gaffer. Obviously this gaffer didn’t get much time to get to know the players, he came late in pre-season. But we are a young team. We are going to make mistakes and it might take us a bit of time to get used to the way he wants to play.

“I’ve got no doubt that the team will go from one strength to another.”

Newcastle have undergone considerable changes recently, and Ramsey will hope to become an influential figure in their midfield.

At 25, he still has plenty of time to revive his career at St James’ Park, but consistent performances will be essential if he wants to justify the substantial investment made in his services.

#1350. Mourinho makes Endrick stance clear following interest from Milan and Roma

Jose Mourinho has made it clear that he does not want to lose hold of Brazilian talent Endrick, who has been linked with January moves to Milan and Roma, but admits that the situation will be beyond his control if the ‘top management’ decides to ‘do something different’.

According to recent reports, Milan are willing to invest €60m on the signing of Endrick in January, and Roma are also said to be interested in the event that the Brazilian becomes available for loan.

Mourinho, meanwhile, has made it clear that he ‘needs’ Endrick at his disposal, but has admitted that the final say is not his to make.

“Look, for me, the situation is very clear. For me, Real Madrid is much more important than Endrick. I love Endrick very much, I care about him a lot, he’s a fantastic guy. Real Madrid needs him, the Real Madrid coach needs him,” said the Special One (via La Gazzetta dello Sport).

He continued: “There’s your response. You have it, those who write about it have it, the agents have it, the clubs that send stories to the newspapers have it. You have my answer. But, if the top management at Real Madrid, meaning my superiors, decide to do something different, in today’s football, you have to respect it.”

Endrick is not the only player being linked with a move to Milan or Roma, though. Club Brugge’s Nicolo Tresoldi is also of interest to the Rossoneri and Friday’s reports claim that VfB Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic is also an option.

Roma, meanwhile, have been linked with moves for a few other traditional wingers, including Chelsea’s Jamie Bynoe-Gittens and Nottingham Forest’s Callum Hudson-Odoi.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.
