The side led by Cesc Fabregas is impressing both domestically and in Europe, as it is currently fourth in the league-phase standings of the UEFA Champions League. Fabregas can count on some of the best players in the league, such as Nico Paz, the Argentine talent who is now also expected to lead the national team after Lionel Messi's retirement. The question is how far Como can go this season, given that playing every three days can be a big challenge for players who have never experienced it. They may still have to pay the price in the league, but qualifying for at least the playoffs of Europe's elite competition would remain a realistic target and, given the circumstances, a remarkable achievement in itself.

It's always about Manchester City: the Citizens are still waiting to learn what sanctions they will face after an independent commission found them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules. They are facing a challenging season that might have an impact on the years ahead. It's not clear what the sanctions will be, but we will likely know more before the end of the current season. On the pitch, they are also facing a season of changes as longtime coach Pep Guardiola left the club in the summer and was replaced by Enzo Maresca, who is now overseeing that transition.

Spanish soccer is not just about Real Madrid and Barcelona: Atletico Madrid are once again near the top of the standings, five points behind the Blaugrana. Diego Simeone, who has coached the club since 2011, is an Atletico Madrid legend who has faced so many changes over the years but has always been able to recreate the right atmosphere and environment to succeed. Atletico have changed their tactical approach and playing style many times, but they are still near the top, and that is what makes Simeone special.

#1208. How Louisville City plans to tackle rare morning kickoff vs. Sacramento Republic in Saturday's USL final

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In recent years, Louisville City FC have been one of the most successful regular-season teams in United Soccer League history, but it hasn't translated to winning the big game. They haven't won the USL Championship since 2018, and while this season has been a trying time dealing with injuries and a new coach taking over, they're playing their best soccer when it matters to set up a strange clash with Sacramento Republic at noon Eastern on Saturday. What's strange isn't that it's Louisville and Sacramento meeting, but that the match kicks off at 9 a.m. local time, a time Louisville forward Ray Serrano says he hasn't played soccer at since he was 15. While it's a regular training time for Louisville and they'll try to keep things on an East Coast timeline, it's hard not to take the shift into account when planning for a final.

It's a challenge that comes with the desire to reach as many fans as possible with a final of this magnitude. Leagues have to work with broadcast networks to ensure that the slots work, and for the USL, having the game on CBS is worth the risk of a 9 a.m. local start with a West Coast team hosting. It's nothing Louisville won't be prepared for, as they look to keep their internal clocks on Eastern Standard Time.

"No, we're trying to stay on Eastern Time, so for us, it's training time," defender Kyle Adams said. "Wake up at 8:00 a.m., but really it's 5:00 a.m. Go to sleep a little bit earlier. Try to do everything really just to stay on Eastern Time, eat a little bit earlier on the night before, and just treat it as going into training, and then get after them."

Other teams have dealt with similar issues, like the Los Angeles Rams when playing an NFL game in Australia, but it's still a struggle to deal with en route to a cup final as Louisville look to reach the pinnacle of the sport for the first time since 2018. Winners of the Prinx Tires USL Cup during the regular season, they do have cup experience that will prove to be fruitful in this competition, which Adams noted has been something that brings the injury-riddled squad together. "We know in the last few years we've struggled in these knockout games, but this year we've turned it on," Serrano said. "It has been really good preparation, just the mentality of going into them, how we deal with the pressure, and we're seeing the fruits of all that now."

It's cliche to say that because of the adversity that they've dealt with, the club is playing its best soccer when it matters, but between using four goalkeepers during the season and seeing manager Danny Cruz depart to be an assistant manager with Minnesota United, it hasn't been an easy task for interim manager Simon Bird to get this team on the right track at this critical juncture.

"Going back to the main part is the adversity that we've faced. You mentioned injuries, having to deal with that side of it, some of the various parts of the season, different things we've had to deal with from a tactical or technical standpoint, where we've lost games, and we feel that we shouldn't have lost games," Bird said when reflecting on the team's development under his leadership. "The most impressive thing I said to the guys today, yesterday in training, we worked on our defensive structure, but the whole training session I thought was excellent, not just the defensive side, off the ball but with the ball, and to see it all come together towards the end of the season is really rewarding. Hopefully, we can carry that on and put together a complete performance, and that's what we've had throughout the season-moments where we've let ourselves down in all these different areas, set pieces, maybe transition at other times, in front of goal. So, putting it all together for a complete performance on Saturday is the goal."

Traveling away to a tough environment in Heart Health Park, Louisville will meet the hottest team in the league in Sacramento Republic. They've ridden a club-record 16-game unbeaten run to the final based on their defense. That has set a strong foundation to build on, and it could make the final one where the first team to score a goal wins the match. Sacramento's squad also has experience in USL Cup finals, which goes a long way when preparing for games of this stature.

"I don't think it can hurt to have that. This would be a step forward for my first final. I think experience is invaluable for players and for staff," Sacramento coach Neil Collins said. "But then there's also the recognition that every game is different, every team is different, and every season is different. So it's just trying to get the balance right and enjoy the opportunity. You've got to have the mechanisms to control the things you can control. Obviously, the opposition team is trying to do the same, and we've got to do everything we can to be ready to take the opportunity when it comes. But the experience will definitely help us; there's plenty of that in our dressing room."

It's a final where the best that the league has to offer will be on display, and it couldn't come at a better time. The summer of soccer, with the United States hosting the World Cup alongside Mexico and Canada, has truly turned into a soccer avalanche, and this final showcases one of the top atmospheres in the league. You can't ask for much better than that, as no matter what, a drought will come to an end. Sacramento Republic haven't won the final since 2014, while Louisville haven't won since 2018, and for these clubs, it will mean a lot to get back to the top.

#1207. How to make AI data centres more sustainable

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M. Santiago/Getty

Around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency says.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

There are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

But none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that new energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

One solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

There is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

These are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

There are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

#1205. Inside the crime epidemic striking fear into Premier League stars: Terrified players paying 'protection money' and buying £20,000 guard dogs, WAGs targeted in violent carjackings and the fall of the crime family who targeted Alexander Isak

Published: 12:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 04:24 EST, 20 November 2026

The man parked up in a nondescript green Ford Fiesta cut an incongruous sight in the affluent residential neighbourhood of Casal Palocco, in south-west Rome, but no one paid him much notice. He made no eye contact and at no stage stepped from the car.

It was only after the street’s famous resident, AS Roma’s Belgian midfielder Radja Nainggolan, had his home burgled and an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions stolen that the player’s then wife, Claudia, six months pregnant at that time in April 2016, recalled the Eastern European-looking man in the battered vehicle up their street.

He was Vlada Djuric, a 50-year-old Macedonian of Romani descent and part of the wider Nikolov family, including his wife Zora Jovanovic, their two sons and daughter, whose highly organised thefts from the homes of top footballers would continue for more than a decade, with imprisonment deemed only a minor setback.

While the Nainggolans were blithely unaware of the criminal family’s lookout man – they’d gone to visit friends nearby for a couple of hours and hadn't even bothered to activate the burglar alarm – the assailants were primed to seize the chance.

The two sons, Valentino and Giacomo, mounted the villa’s perimeter wall, opening one door with a magnetic card and jimmying another with a screwdriver, and proceeded undisturbed through the house in 27 minutes, throwing the proceeds of their burglary into a bag as they went.

There were 15 watches (Rolex, Patek Philippe and others) valued at £250,000 and 20 pieces of jewellery, including a diamond worth £25,000. Security cameras on a landing and in an internal room filmed them but such was their confidence, they only partially covered their faces.

Former Roma midfielder Radja Nainggolan and his then wife Claudia, who was six months pregnant, were the targets of a burglary in 2016 (Source: Instagram/Claudia_lai_82)

Nainggolan had an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions taken, including 15 watches

It was old-fashioned detective work from a local officer, Bruno Failla, which led police to a rambling home at Lurano, a small town six hours drive away in Lombardy, at which the Nikolovs would lavishly entertain other members of the Romani community.

The watches matched the descriptions of those stolen from the Nainggolans, though it was a necklace with a Roma logo, and the pair of red shoes with Nainggolan's initials, which really gave the game away.

‘I ask again for vigilance and watchfulness, please,’ Failla said at the time, because this was the fourth time that footballers' properties in Casal Palocco had been targeted in the space of five years. But the challenge of placing footballers in a state of constant vigilance became clear fully seven years on, when another Nainggolan residence, in Antwerp, Belgium, was burgled while his relatives held a party there.

‘It is one of the most complicated and consistently challenging parts of our security work,’ one former special forces soldier now providing security for footballers tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s been a big sector of our work for years now, but the movements of these clients are so public and that’s irresistible to criminals. The wealth is very evident.’

One of the sons, Valentino, was jailed for two years in 2016 and other members of his family also did time, but once out, they all set their sights on the Premier League. In 2024, they arrived in the UK via a ferry to Dover from Calais, stopped off in London and made their way north, sleeping in a Ford motorhome and travelling to target homes in a Citroen C3.

A spree of attacks ensued from them on the homes of Alexander Isak, then a Newcastle player, Wolves’ Matheus Cunha (who has subsequently been burgled again while at Manchester United), Birmingham City’s Neil Etheridge and Leon Bailey, with Aston Villa at the time.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, Everton and United, are known to have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of players who are in squads playing away from home – rather than have that in the hands of a range of private operators.

Some of the top football TV analysts are known to have sought the same security cover outside their houses when away at games.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of stars who are playing away

Three masked criminals managed to slip over Bruno Fernandes' security fence and into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and made off with jewellery

It didn’t work in the case of Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes. Three masked criminals still managed to slip over the security fence into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and make off with jewellery.

It was one of the player’s neighbours who spotted them on their CCTV system and alerted police, who arrived five minutes after the burglars had left. Some in this security sector feel that it takes the private firms' former military and special services experience to cope with the criminal gangs’ level of sophistication.

Clubs using security staff in this way is a relatively recent development. In the days of security officers like United’s Ned Kelly, who wrote a book about his 14 years with the club, the job entailed ensuring the team were protected in public, or ferrying managers and new signings around.

Many clubs still leave it to players. ‘Player-liaison staff will recommend vetted security providers but it’s down to player personal choice for obvious reasons,’ says one player agent.

'That's not always been easy,' says a former Premier League player-liaison officer. 'The players have a huge entourage: so-called experts who want a seat at the table and think they know best. Of course, social media enhances the security problem.'

The house burglars’ modus operandi pales by comparison with some of violence displayed by others who prey on the footballer set. One footballer's wife in Cheshire was driving a top-of-the-range vehicle when a moped took up a position in front of her and slowed. In her rear-view mirror, she saw a second. The driver of the third then arrived at her side window, assessing what there was to steal.

On any given day, there could have been £200,000 worth of jewellery in the car, though she was wearing neither rings nor a watch on this occasion. The three drove off.

The episode had echoes of the attempted heist which saw Arsenal’s Mesut Ozil and Sead Kolasinac carjacked in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago.

Sead Kolasinac, then of Arsenal, thwarts an attempted carjacking in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago. Kolasinac was with his team-mate Mesut Ozil at the time

Attackers go for Kolasinac after his car was 'boxed in' when approaching traffic lights

Paul Hughes, managing director of Benchmark Security Group, a leading Manchester-based protection firm, employs former police and Royal security drivers to train his clients in the art of 'defensive driving'.

In a two-hour session, they learn how to avoid being 'boxed in' – as Ozil and Kolasinac were – when approaching traffic lights. Techniques include never taking up a position in the middle lane, avoiding the outside lane if there is a central barrier, and always maintaining sight of the tyres of the vehicle in front when you slow.

'If you can see the tyres, you will always have room to manoeuvre right or left of the car in front, at speed, without hitting it,' Hughes says.

His staff are often asked to escort clients in their fleet of vehicles, which includes two Land Rovers with blacked-out windows. The firm acquired a Darkfighter Dome – a night-vision camera which is mounted on to the roof of its security vehicles – allowing them to see would-be assailants in the dark. Escorted school runs are also part of the protection they offer.

A screen which dominates Benchmark's underground headquarters, at anonymous premises in Manchester, revealed the fortresses that players' houses have become, when I visited.

It showed live feeds from the gardens of mansions which are criss-crossed by infra-red beams. An alarm is triggered in the control room if anyone not approved through face-recognition software is picked up by up to 18 pan, tilt and zoom cameras at a property.

Loudspeakers, operated from the control room, warn off intruders. A team of security staff is never more than six minutes away. A patrol is on the scene of an alert, usually within 90 seconds.

A number of Manchester United players have invested in specialised security dogs from the Leicester-based firm Chaperone K9 at a cost of up to £20,000 each, though some sources suggest demand has receded as many players have young children. Security firms have their own dogs.

Benchmark are one of Britain's most trusted operators – industry-accredited, with former senior police officers on their staff. But this is also a world in which some unsavoury individuals are looking to extract gain.

Daily Mail Sport is aware that a number of current players have paid protection money to ensure they remain safe and are not venturing out socially without having done so. The ‘panic rooms’ some install in their homes, with security card access, are a place to hide valuables.

The family who preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. Valentino Nikolov (pictured) is serving an initial 10-year sentence, which has since been extended

Kolasinac fought off the carjackers. Everton's Duncan Ferguson put an assailant in hospital when he tried to burgle his home at Ormskirk, Lancashire, in January 2001. ‘I’m not a hard man off the pitch...unless you try to break into my house,’ he said recently.

But the assailants in the Ozil and Kolasinac attack were part of Eastern European gangs. 'The criminal demographic has changed,' one former senior detective tells me. 'We are now talking about gangs who lack the slightest compunction about taking a life.'

The Italian family who have preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. The Rome lookout man’s two sons were jailed for 10 years and eight years respectively at Newcastle Crown Court last year, for burglaries including the Isak attack – sentences since extended. Their mother is doing seven years.

That court case revealed how the family had moved on from the days of old cars, screwdrivers and shinning over walls in Rome – using Isak’s own vehicle as a battering ram to force entry to his Newcastle home.

'None of the property stolen from my home was ever recovered,’ Isak related. 'The attack left me with a sense of unease and a fear it could reoccur.'

#1204. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. In his pre-match press conference Arteta noted concerns about Noni Madueke (ankle), Declan Rice (thigh). Riccardo Calafiori (unspecified) and Christos Tzolis who has returned to training but all are expected to be available. Andoni Iraola has ruled out Jeremie Frimpong as well as long-term casualties Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley but hopes to be able to include Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz. #1202. EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

#1198. Revealed: Tottenham's aggressive youth recruitment campaign to snap up Britain's best teenage stars and blow rivals out of the water - with the help of expensive private schools and lucrative pro deals

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026

Tottenham Hotspur have launched an aggressive campaign to recruit Britain's most talented young footballers from rivals, using expensive private education and lucrative professional contracts to lure them in.

Daily Mail Sport can reveal Spurs are targeting the country's most talented Under 15s through a bespoke package, headed by hefty wages when youngsters turn professional aged 17 and free education at one of the country's finest private schools.

And a glimpse of what the future might look like came against Crystal Palace on October 31.

With Tottenham 2-0 up, Roberto De Zerbi introduced 18-year-old academy graduate Luca Williams-Barnett in the 88th minute. The eye-catching cameo proved a memorable Premier League debut, and last week earned him the top flight's Creative Moment of the Month award for a mazy dribble through Palace's defence.

It's further evidence of the talent coming through at Spurs. Williams-Barnett is not a product of the new recruitment drive, but he offers an illustration of what the club hope to achieve by nurturing talented youngsters and giving them opportunities in the first team.

That has not always been Tottenham's strength, having endured a decade of failing to turn potential into established first-team players. Since Harry Kane and Andros Townsend made their league debuts in 2012, only three Spurs academy graduates – Ryan Mason, Harry Winks and Oliver Skipp – have made at least 30 Premier League appearances for the club.

A glimpse of what Tottenham's future might look like came against Crystal Palace on October 31 with Luca Williams-Barnett's thrilling cameo off the bench

Since Harry Kane and Andros Townsend (left) made their debuts, only Harry Winks, Ryan Mason (right) and Oliver Skipp have made 30 top-flight appearances from Spurs' academy

In a Daily Mail Sport interview last month, ex-Spurs player and manager Tim Sherwood claimed Tottenham's inability to give youngsters a proper pathway to the first team has failed those in the set-up over the past decade, and that the academy may as well be 'closed up'.

It is a record the club are determined to change. Spurs' renewed strategy has been felt across the Premier League's academy circuit over the past year, with rivals anxious at what lies ahead.

The competition for young players is growing. As well as the traditional Big Six clubs, Newcastle, Aston Villa and Brighton have also become worthy competitors because of the first-team pathways they offer.

Tottenham pay £21,000-a-year fees to St John's Senior School in Enfield, which boasts top grades and facilities. Its most recent GCSE cohort achieved 65.3 per cent grades 9–7, formerly known as A* and A grades. The school's football pitch has 22 water cannons underneath (the same number as Arsenal's Emirates Stadium) and both primary and secondary drainage systems.

The programme presented to the parents of prospective stars is the key selling point. Spurs have been given permission by the league to provide a Full-Time Training Module (FTTM) programme which allows students more time away from school. They have their lessons at St John's but on three days a week after lunch, they go to the training ground and focus on football. It is the school's responsibility to organise catch-up lessons so education is not missed out on.

Arsenal, Manchester City, Brighton and Wolves were the first adopters of FTTM, and now Spurs have joined them. Where Tottenham have elevated their strategy is in the number of schoolboys whose fees they cover. Daily Mail Sport understands Spurs have awarded multiple FTTMs to pupils, covering fees in excess of £300,000 annually.

Through this, the club have been able to lure in some of the country's best talents. Isaac Allen, who has captained the England Under 15s, joined Spurs from West Ham in August despite Arsenal's attempts to sign him. The 15-year-old struck four goals in three matches at the Under-15 World Cup last month. Gabriel Rigg, 15, was also recruited from West Ham in September, while Spurs beat Arsenal, Chelsea and Newcastle to the signing of Jake Maloney, 14, from Charlton.

The most promising among the cohort is Ashiah Haughton-Sinclair, who in September trained with Spurs' first team. Last season the 15-year-old became the youngest player to feature for their Under 18s, and netted 70 goals and 20 assists.

Troy Parrott (right) came through the youth set-up but struggled for game time behind Kane. He left for AZ Alkmaar in 2024, and this summer signed for Real Betis

Marcus Edwards (right) is another Spurs academy product who made the grade elsewhere, scoring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium for Sporting Lisbon in 2022

Spurs' Hotspur Way base, opened in 2012, is renowned as being one of the finest training complexes in European football, and is regularly used by the England team

Tottenham's ambitions didn't stop there, as they tried to recruit other players from rivals last summer. The club thought Kyran Thompson was joining from Arsenal, before Newcastle snapped up the talented forward at the last minute. Mishel Nduka, also previously at Arsenal, was approached by Tottenham before he chose a lucrative deal at Manchester City.

Daily Mail Sport understands Spurs pay higher salaries than most Premier League clubs – bar Man City and Chelsea – for academy stars signing professional terms aged 17, which is the earliest age allowed.

This is a significant bargaining chip, as many clubs are rigid in what they will offer players signing their first professional contract.

There is typically the belief that too much, too young can have a negative impact, but Spurs view it as a necessary ingredient in the modern competition for talent. Nurturing academy graduates into the first team negates the need to spend millions later down the line on established players.

The Tottenham aim is for their first team in the next five years to be reinforced by multiple leading academy graduates, after a decade of producing promising talent – such as Marcus Edwards and Troy Parrott, now at Burnley and Real Betis respectively – without giving them a viable pathway at the club.

And those surplus to requirements could be sold for substantial fees. Luka Vuskovic (£50million to Brighton), Will Lankshear (£20m to Middlesbrough), Ashley Phillips (£20m to Middlesbrough) and Alfie Devine (£6m to Preston North End) are recent examples.

Facilities play a part, too. Spurs' Hotspur Way base, opened in 2012, is renowned as one of the finest training complexes in European football.

The 77-acre state-of-the-art complex in Enfield, which cost £45m to build in 2012 and has since seen significant investment, is home to both the first team and academy, as well as being used regularly by England.

Luka Vuskovic was snapped up before his price tag got too high, and then was sold to Brighton for £50million this summer when he couldn't break into the starting line-up

Will Lankshear earned Spurs another £20m when he left for Middlesbrough

With Williams-Barnett already offering a glimpse of what lies ahead, Spurs will hope he is the first of many academy graduates to make the leap

While four of the 15 grass pitches are reserved exclusively for first-team training, the youngsters benefit from being immersed in the same elite environment as the senior professionals they aspire to emulate. It's an arrangement designed to make the pathway from youth prospect to Premier League footballer feel that little bit closer.

With Williams-Barnett already offering a glimpse of what lies ahead, Spurs will hope he is the first of many academy graduates to make the leap, rather than another reminder of the potential they have previously allowed to slip through their fingers.

For a club that has spent the best part of a decade searching for its next homegrown star, the teenager could yet become the face of a long-overdue academy revival.
